verdict.winner: Natural slate and clay tile lead for NJ historic homes on in-kind authenticity and 100+-year durability; cedar shingle and copper match specific period styles, with synthetic slate the budget alternate.
verdict.reasoning: Natural slate leads because it is the in-kind original roof on Victorian, Colonial Revival, and Gilded Age homes and lasts 60-150 years (premium 100+ per the National Slate Association), satisfying Standard 6's directive to replace a distinctive roof in kind, per the NPS; clay tile matches it at 100+ years on Spanish and Mission styles, per the InterNACHI chart.
verdict.alternate: Synthetic slate is the alternate when natural slate is cost-prohibitive — simulated slate lasts 10-35 years per InterNACHI, composite lines 40-50 years per CertainTeed — though some Historic Preservation Commissions require natural stone; cedar shingle remains the in-kind choice for Craftsman-era homes, per the Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau and NPS Brief 19.

keyFacts: Natural slate lasts 60-150 years per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart, with premium slate 100+ years per the National Slate Association.
Clay tile lasts 100+ years per the InterNACHI chart, often 75+ and many 100+ per the TRI Alliance.
Copper lasts 70+ years per the InterNACHI chart, and over 100 years on a properly installed standing-seam, batten-seam, or flat-seam roof per the Copper Development Association.
Cedar shake lasts 20-40 years and cedar shingle 30-50 years per the Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau.
Synthetic (simulated) slate lasts 10-35 years per the InterNACHI chart, with composite lines designed to 40-50 years per CertainTeed.
Architectural asphalt shingles last 25-35 years per GAF and install at $6.50-$11.00 per square foot in NJ per Josten Roofing.
Standard 6 of the Secretary of the Interior's Standards directs that a distinctive historic roof be replaced in kind — matched in design, color, and texture — per the National Park Service.

Natural slate is repaired rather than replaced whenever possible per NPS Preservation Brief 29, with non-ferrous solid-copper or stainless-steel fasteners required because plain or galvanized steel rusts out before the slate; the roof is replaced only when 20% or more of slates are broken, missing, or sliding, per Brief 29.

Clay tile is matched in profile, color, glaze, and texture (Spanish, Mission/barrel, pantile, or flat English shingle) per NPS Preservation Brief 30 and fastened with copper nails or hangers, since original copper nails replaced with iron nails corrode and trigger roof failure.

Cedar shingle replacement matches the original size, shape, texture, and exposure rather than an aged look per NPS Preservation Brief 19, and uses hot-dipped zinc-coated, aluminum, or stainless-steel nails — not copper — because a chemical reaction between red cedar and copper shortens the roof's life.

Natural slate suits Victorian, Colonial Revival, and Gilded Age homes; clay tile suits Spanish Revival and Mission-style homes; cedar shingle suits Craftsman, bungalow, and early Colonial homes; copper suits Federal, Greek Revival, and farmhouse styles, per NPS Preservation Brief 4.
Historic metals named in NPS Preservation Brief 4 are tin plate, terne plate, copper, lead, and zinc.
Brief 4 directs that historic fabric (roof coursing, color variation) be photographed, measured, and recorded before work begins for future reference.

Synthetic slate and architectural asphalt substitute only on non-character-defining roofs — primarily flat or non-visible sections, or non-contributing structures — per NPS Preservation Brief 4, since asphalt is not a like-for-like swap for a visible historic roof.
sources: National Park Service (NPS) — Secretary of the Interior's Standards, Standard 6
NPS Preservation Brief 4 (roofing of historic buildings)
njContext: A Certificate of Appropriateness — not National Register or NJ Register listing — is the binding gate on a private NJ reroof, required for a designated landmark or a property in a LOCAL historic district per N.J.S.A. 40:55D-107.

A Certificate of Appropriateness does not replace a building permit; a reroof in a local district commonly needs both, and the NJ Uniform Construction Code treats a full re-roof of a detached 1- or 2-family dwelling as ordinary maintenance with no construction permit per N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7.

National Register or NJ Register listing alone places no restriction on a private owner using private funds — the NPS states listing 'places no federal restrictions or requirements on a private property owner,' and the NJ DEP HPO states listing 'does not place restrictions on private property owner rights'; the binding control is the local ordinance and its Certificate of Appropriateness.

Essex County local-district controls: Glen Ridge regulates a district covering over 90% of the Borough under Borough Code Ch. 15.32; Montclair under Code §347-136; Newark's Landmarks and Historic Preservation Commission auto-designated Register-listed districts as of May 30, 2007.

Natural slate and cedar shingle suit a designated Essex County historic house matched in kind under Standard 6 — slate on a pre-1920 Montclair or Newark home, cedar on a Craftsman — per the NPS Preservation Briefs.

Cedar shingle on an Essex County Craftsman home is fastened with hot-dipped zinc-coated, aluminum, or stainless-steel nails (not copper) per NPS Preservation Brief 19, and fire-retardant-treated cedar meets local Class B or C code where required.

The federal 20% Historic Rehabilitation Tax Credit (IRC §47) applies only to depreciable income-producing buildings — owner-occupied residences do not qualify per the NPS and NJ HPO — claimed ratably over 5 years, eligibility set by a tax professional, the NPS, and NJEDA.

The NJ Historic Property Reinvestment Program (NJEDA) is limited to income-producing properties; a residential project runs as rental with at least four dwelling units, keyed to a qualifying historic designation and the Secretary of the Interior's Standards.
The pending NJ homeowner historic credit (S3545) is not law.
positioning: Position Newark Quality Roofing as a registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor (registration under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136 — NJ has no separate roofing license), insured, offering a free written estimate, that installs period-appropriate historic roofing (natural slate, clay tile, cedar shingle, copper) matched in kind to the Secretary of the Interior's Standards and any local Certificate-of-Appropriateness review. NQR handles the roofing scope — documenting and matching original material, profile, and fasteners per the applicable NPS Preservation Brief — and coordinates with the local Historic Preservation Commission; it does not determine tax-credit eligibility (a tax professional, the NPS, and NJEDA do that). Warranty framing is honest and two-part: a manufacturer material warranty plus NQR's own written workmanship warranty — never manufacturer-certification tiers (no GAF Master Elite / CertainTeed SELECT ShingleMaster claims) and never 'licensed.'
